summary: Documents the extended TACACS protocol used by Cisco terminal servers, which lets a server check with a central system whether a user may log in or use a device. The University of Minnesota used the same protocol for its distributed authentication.

eli5.summary: A guard at a door asks the main office whether a visitor is allowed in. TACACS is how a network device asks a central computer the same thing.

subtitle: A protocol for delegating authentication decisions to a central server

tldr.problem: Terminal servers need a way to check with a central authority before allowing a user to log in, rather than storing credentials locally.
tldr.mechanism: TACACS defines request/response messages where a terminal server sends a login attempt to an authentication daemon, which decides whether to allow access and can return additional parameters.
tldr.outcome: Cisco Systems terminal servers and the University of Minnesota's distributed authentication system use TACACS to centralize access control decisions while letting each access point remain stateless.

today: RFC 1492 is informational and describes the extended TACACS protocol as implemented by Cisco and the University of Minnesota. It has not been updated or obsoleted. However, RADIUS and TACACS+ have become more widely adopted for distributed authentication in later years, though TACACS remains in use in legacy Cisco systems.

sections.title: The Authentication Delegation Problem
sections.content:
In the early days of the ARPANET, dial-up access was controlled through specialized devices called TIPs (Terminal Interface Processors). These devices needed a way to determine which users were permitted to connect. Rather than storing a password file on each TIP, the network could offload the authentication decision to a central TACACS daemon running on a host computer.

This RFC documents the extended TACACS protocol used by Cisco Systems terminal servers and the University of Minnesota's distributed authentication system. The protocol allows a client device (such as a terminal server) to send authentication requests to a server daemon, which evaluates the request and returns a decision.
sections.eli5: A terminal server accepts a username and password from someone trying to log in. Instead of deciding on its own, the server asks a central computer: 'Is this person allowed in?' The TACACS protocol defines how to ask that question and get an answer back.

sections.title: TACACS Request and Response Types
sections.content:
TACACS defines several types of requests that a client can send. The AUTH request asks whether a username and password are valid. The LOGIN request both authenticates a user and signals that a login session is starting; it can return three result values that the client can use for local policy decisions.

The CONNECT request asks, in the context of an existing login session, whether the user is permitted to open a TCP connection to a specific IP address and port. The SUPERUSER request asks whether a user can enter privileged mode on the terminal server. The LOGOUT request signals that a session is ending. For SLIP connections, there are SLIPADDR, SLIPON, and SLIPOFF requests to manage IP address assignment and session state.

All requests must receive a response; the server indicates either acceptance or rejection, and may include a reason code explaining why a request was denied.
sections.eli5: TACACS messages ask different questions: 'Is this password correct?' 'Can this user open a connection to that computer?' 'Can they use admin features?' The server always answers yes or no, and can explain why if it says no.

sections.title: Two Encoding Formats
sections.content:
TACACS supports two different encoding schemes. The UDP encoding uses User Datagram Protocol and port 49, and is compatible with the original TACACS specification. Requests are simple binary packets with fixed and variable-length fields. The packet includes a version field (0 for simple form, 128 for extended), a type field indicating the request kind, a nonce value to match responses with requests, username and password lengths, response codes, result fields, and the actual username and password data.

The TCP encoding is a modern alternative that sends requests as four lines of ASCII text: the version and type, the username, the password, and the line number. Responses follow RFC 821 SMTP-style reply codes (like '201 accepted' or '502 access denied'). The ASCII format is easier to implement, especially on systems with limited UDP support, and allows more flexible error reporting.
sections.eli5: TACACS can send messages in two ways: as compact binary packets using UDP, or as readable text lines using TCP. The TCP version is simpler to program but slightly larger; the UDP version is more compact but harder to code.

sections.title: Security and Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that TACACS sends usernames and passwords in clear text within either a UDP packet or TCP stream. This means that an attacker who can monitor network traffic between the client and server can capture credentials. The RFC recommends using point-to-point links, physically securing transmission media, and using secure routing to prevent unauthorized packet capture.

The TACACS daemon can implement sophisticated policies beyond simple password checking. Implementations might use alternate password files, access databases, SecureID cards, or even translate requests to other protocols like Kerberos. A 'fanout' server can centralize logging and policy enforcement, allowing administrators to block specific users or poor passwords across all access points.

The protocol is flexible enough to support various real-world scenarios. Username format can indicate an authentication style to apply. Result values returned from LOGIN and CONNECT requests can convey access list identifiers or other policy parameters that the terminal server interprets locally.
sections.eli5: TACACS sends passwords in plain text, so it only works safely if the connection is private and secure. The great advantage is that the authentication server can be very smart: it can check many databases, enforce complex rules, and log everything in one place.

sections.title: Real-World Usage at the University of Minnesota
sections.content:
The RFC includes a detailed case study of how the University of Minnesota implemented TACACS-based authentication. Usernames follow a format like 'First.M.Last-#@umn.edu', which the central system converts to an email address 'user@host'. The central fanout server validates that requests come from permitted client devices, checks usernames for invalid characters, looks up user information in the university directory, and consults a blocked list. It then forwards the request to an appropriate validation host specified by the username.

For database access, the system can return the user's staff status from the directory, allowing selective access based on organizational role. Different pools of lines (for example, 800-number dial-in lines versus regular modem pool) can have different permitted users and validation hosts. This demonstrates how TACACS can support sophisticated, distributed authorization policies while keeping the terminal server itself stateless.
sections.eli5: In practice, a university used TACACS to ask a central directory: 'Is this person a staff member?' and 'Are they allowed to use this modem line?' The central server could look up the answer in databases and remember which users were blocked.
